Title: A survey on resource scheduling approaches in multi-access edge computing environment: a deep reinforcement learning study
Text:
A survey on resource scheduling approaches in multi-access edge
computing environment: a deep reinforcement learning study
Ahmed A. Ismail1 • Nour Eldeen Khalifa1 • Reda A. El-Khoribi1
Received: 5 May 2024 / Revised: 4 November 2024 / Accepted: 7 November 2024 / Published online: 21 January 2025
 The Author(s) 2024
Abstract
Multi-access edge computing (MEC) brings many services closer to user devices, alleviating the pressure on resource-
constrained devices. It enables devices to ofﬂoad compute-intensive tasks to nearby MEC servers. Hence, improving users’
quality of experience (QoS) by reducing both application execution time and energy consumption. However, to meet the
huge demands, efﬁcient resource scheduling algorithms are an essential and challenging problem. Resource scheduling
involves efﬁciently allocating and managing MEC resources. In this paper, we survey the state-of-the-art research
regarding this issue and focus on deep reinforcement learning (DRL) solutions. DRL algorithms reach optimal or near-
optimal policies when adapted to a particular scenario. To the best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst survey that speciﬁcally
focuses on the use of RL and DRL techniques for resource scheduling in multi-access computing. We analyze recent
literature in three research aspects, namely, content caching, computation ofﬂoading, and resource management. Moreover,
we compare and classify the reviewed papers in terms of application use cases, network architectures, objectives, utilized
RL algorithms, evaluation metrics, and model approaches: centralized and distributed. Furthermore, we investigate the
issue of user mobility and its effect on the model. Finally, we point out a few unresolved research challenges and suggest
several open research topics for future studies.

1 Introduction
With the rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) and
the prosperous development of 5G wireless networks,
numerous new applications are emerging, such as face
recognition, wearable devices, virtual reality (VR), augmented
reality (AR), the internet of vehicles (IoV), and self-driving
vehicles (SDV). It is estimated that by 2025, there will be over
75 billion IoT devices worldwide [1]. All these devices need
resources to fully collaborate to provide desired applications
[1, 2]. Moreover, most IoT devices and mobile devices (MDs)
are resource-constrained devices that have limited processing
power and storage capacity. They cannot provide resources for
delay-sensitive applications. The application-intensive tasks
can put a heavy load on the processor and reduce battery life
[3]. Two new paradigms are proposed to address these issues:
mobile cloud computing (MCC) and multi-access edge com-
puting (MEC), aimed at enhancing the capabilities of mobile
devices and IoT devices by leveraging cloud or edge resources.
However, they differ in their approaches and where compu-
tation and data processing occur.
MCC was initially introduced to alleviate the resource
bottleneck [4]. MCC enables the execution of mobile
applications outside mobile devices in the cloud connected
to the mobile network. MCC was very popular for mobile
cloud applications. Although MCC has gained popularity
for mobile cloud applications, the centralization of the
cloud can lead to increased physical distance between the

Scalability: Deep neural networks, which are used in DRL

Addressing real-world problems with substantial data and
computing requirements beneﬁts from its scalability.
•
Applicable to distinct domains: It can handle numerous
applications including, industries, robotics, banking,
healthcare, natural language processing (NLP), gaming,

3.1 Recent advances in MEC network (RQ1)
Multi-access edge computing aims to enhance cloud
computing capabilities by providing services closer to
users at the network’s edge. Edge servers are typically
deployed in cellular base stations or small cells. Users can
access the MEC system through various technologies
including Wi-Fi, LTE, and 5G [16]. The compatibility of
edge servers with various network environments is a sig-
niﬁcant factor that driving their use in future networks.
MEC architecture, as shown in Fig. 2, consists of three
tiers. The ﬁrst tier, known as the ‘‘thing layer,’’ includes all
user devices. The second tier called the ‘‘edge layer,’’
consists of edge servers deployed at the base station or
gateway. The third tier is the ‘‘cloud layer.’’ MEC networks
enable collaboration and cooperation between devices in
multitier architectures such as things-edge collaboration,
things-edge-cloud collaboration, edge-edge collaboration,
and edge-cloud collaboration [17].
Additionally, new developments in MEC systems are
being implemented to accommodate a variety of devices.

3.2 MEC resource scheduling issues
This subsection addresses the question in RQ2 regarding
resource scheduling in the MEC environment. MEC
resources include Communication, Computing, and Cach-
ing (3Cs). Resource scheduling involves efﬁciently allo-
cating computing resources at the edge to meet the
demands of various applications and services. Many MDs
have applications that are composed of hundreds or thou-
sands of computing-intensive or data-intensive tasks with
different durations and resource requirements. Therefore,
MDs need to ofﬂoad computation to edge servers to alle-
viate the burden of computing-intensive tasks.
However, this will lead to several challenges in MEC.
The ﬁrst challenge is how to handle contention and provide
resources for several devices. A second challenge is how
the edge devices should coordinate with each other and the
cloud, under heterogeneous processing capabilities, to
ensure good end-to-end application-level performance.
Finally, privacy remains a challenge, as some data still
needs to be exchanged between edge devices and possibly
the cloud [11].
Due to these challenges, effective optimization algo-
rithms are required to address resource utilization, mini-
mize latency, and improve the overall performance of edge
environments to accommodate as many requests as possi-
ble. Many solutions have been proposed over the years to
solve the problem of resource scheduling since most of
these problems are NP-hard. Algorithms, such as cooper-
ative or non-cooperative games, Markov decision pro-
cesses
(MDPs),
combinatorial
optimization
problems,
genetic algorithms, multi-stage heuristic algorithms, sim-
ulated annealing algorithms, particle swarm algorithms,
etc.
Since optimization problems often need many iterations
to achieve an acceptable solution, the previously men-
tioned methods are unsuitable for real-time decision-mak-
ing. To handle the issue, it is frequently necessary to adjust
to environments that change over time. DRL methods can
cope with these issues.

in resource scheduling, namely, content caching, compu-

problems in MEC.
3.2.1 Mobile edge caching
The explosion of IoT applications has led to an increase in
data trafﬁc in recent years; the majority of IoT applications
adhere to a content-oriented paradigm. However, the cur-

3.2.2 Computation offloading properties
Real-time and delay-sensitive applications need huge
resources to be capable of processing. However, end
devices such as sensors, cameras, and smartphones have
limited computing and storage capacity. Processing tasks
on such energy-constrained devices becomes even more
complex. Hence, computation ofﬂoading (CO) may be an
appropriate solution for such applications, and edge com-
puting brings resources closer to end devices, which makes
it appropriate for users. Computation ofﬂoading to the edge
environment can reduce energy consumption and task
response time, especially for delay-sensitive applications
[31].
The ofﬂoading problem involves two parts: (1) whether
the tasks need to be ofﬂoaded; and (2) to which edge server
the tasks are ofﬂoaded. However, the process of compu-
tation ofﬂoading is a multi-objective, NP-hard optimization
problem. It can be modeled as a complex mathematical
model [32]. Moreover, the ofﬂoading decision depends on
many factors that should be considered, i.e., the location
and mobility of user devices, network conditions, hetero-
geneity of network devices, and user preferences. The
network conditions
include
wireless
channel
quality,
bandwidth capacity, and signal interference.
As shown in Fig. 3, the CO issue can be classiﬁed based
on granularity, type of tasks, direction, and approaches
used. The granularity of ofﬂoading has two main approa-
ches: full and partial ofﬂoading, as shown in Fig. 4. Full
ofﬂoading, which fully ofﬂoads the task to the edge server
or processes it locally on the device, and partial ofﬂoading,
on the other hand, divides the task into two parts: one to
process locally and one in edge servers. Deﬁnitely, partial
ofﬂoading is more complicated than full ofﬂoading because
it considers not only whether and where to ofﬂoad but also
how many percent of a task should be ofﬂoaded [33].
On the other hand, application tasks can be either
independent or dependent, as shown in Fig. 4. Independent
tasks can be processed separately, and their output is
transferred back to user devices. While dependent tasks
depend on each other the input of one is dependent on
output from other tasks to begin which is more complex to
handle and can be modeled as a directed acyclic graph (-
DAG). The direction of ofﬂoading can vary from ofﬂoad-
ing to a single, multi-edge server, edge-cloud, or ofﬂoading
to UAV-MEC, which has a UAV and MEC server. Many
solutions have been provided to that problem over the years
with different approaches [33], but DRL solutions show
remarkable performance.

3.2.3 Service orchestration and resource management
In general, MEC resources offer computation, communi-
cation, and storage resources as their primary resources.
Typically, CPU cycles and resource blocks (VMs/con-
tainers) are referred to as computing resources. While
wireless resources such as the transmission power, band-

task ofﬂoading are part of communication resources. In
order to speed up service response times and minimize
network load, storage resources are employed to cache
popular content at the network’s edge to reduce requests to
content in the cloud.
Resource management is a process of coordination and
supervision of resources performed by service providers.
Resource management includes several aspects, as will be
discussed in sub Sect. 5.3, such as edge server placement,
resource
allocation,
workload

and

3.3 DRL overview
RL techniques are applied for sequential decision-making,
which can be mathematically formulated as a Markov
decision process (MDP). An MDP consists of a set of states
that represent observation of the environment, a set of
actions that can be applied, a transition probability function
that map from any state-action pair to the next states, and a
reward function. Both the future state and reward of the
environment only depend on the current state and the
action taken by the agent.
RL often begins with an unstructured exploration, where
trial and error are used to learn the rules, followed by
exploitation, where a strategy is chosen and optimized
within the learned rules. The RL agent will begin to learn
by interacting with the environment in any state and start to
take action and get immediate rewards, then go to the next
state and so on till ﬁnished. In general, agents try to
determine the best possible correlation between each state-
action combination and its corresponding value or cumu-
lative reward. The agent follows some strategy by which it
takes action in a state. In an MDP, the essential problem is
to ﬁnd the optimal policy that maximizes the long-term
cumulative reward.
RL algorithms can be mainly divided into two cate-
gories: model-based and model-free [13]. As the name
suggests,
a
model-based
system
involves
an
agent
attempting to gain insights into its environments and
building a model of it from its interactions with them. The
model in such cases is well-known. The agent in such a
case is greedy and will always try to perform an action that
will get the maximum reward, irrespective of what that
action may cause.
On the other hand, model-free algorithms deal with
unknown environments. The model-free agents aim to use
experience to understand the effects of their actions. This
type of algorithm will execute a task numerous times and
modify the policy, or the underlying strategy, to achieve
the best possible results based on outcomes. Most com-
munication problems can be modeled as model-free; hence,
an agent tries to choose the best action to increase the
cumulative reward without full knowledge about the
environment and only observations in the current state. The
model-free DRL approaches can be classiﬁed into two
categories: value-based and policy gradient, as shown in
Fig. 5, which is based on [15, 35].
3.3.1 Value-based methods
One of the most well-known value-based methods is Q-
learning, where the agent learns to estimate the expected
future rewards of taking a particular action in a particular
state, which is called the state–action or Q value function.
These value estimates are then used to make decisions
about which actions to take to maximize long-term
rewards. The value-based methods speciﬁcally focus on
estimating the value of different actions or states in the
environment. The value of an action or state is a measure of
how good it is to take that action or be in that state, typi-
cally in terms of expected future rewards. Moreover, to
ensure adequate exploration and exploitation of the action
space, instead of using only a greedy strategy, they use the
2-greedy strategy.
As mentioned in Sect. 1, deep learning makes it possible
for RL to scale to previously unsolvable decision-making
scenarios, such as those with high-dimensional state and
action spaces. The value-based DRL techniques estimate
the Q value for each state-action pair, and the optimal
policy is to select the action with the maximum Q value for
each state. The ﬁrst breakthrough of DRL was when DQN
[36] adopted to learn to play a range of Atari 2600 video
games at a superhuman level, directly from image pixels.
Another success was the development of AlphaGo, a
hybrid DRL system that defeated a human world champion
in Go [37]. Recently, DRL algorithms have been applied to
a wide range of problems, such as robotics, autonomous
driving, computer vision, and natural language processing.
The primary obstacle facing value-based deep rein-
forcement learning is handling continuous action space
difﬁculties; quantization is a commonly employed solution
for this purpose. On the other hand, extremely rough dis-
cretization hides the details about the geometry of the
action space, while extremely ﬁne discretization results
from the dimension problem. The deep value-based algo-
rithms include algorithms such as DQN [36], double DQN

Another category of model-free deep RL is the policy
gradient-based

[41],

gradient approaches is to update the policy in a way that
maximizes the probability of choosing actions that result in
greater rewards by utilizing the gradient of the predicted
cumulative reward concerning the policy parameters.
Mostly, methods like stochastic gradient ascent are used for
this known in RL as the REINFORCE rule [42], in which
the policy parameters are changed to maximize the
predicted payoff. One of the well-known policy gradient
methods is proximal policy optimization (PPO) [43], which
is an algorithm designed to preserve stability throughout

sure that modiﬁcations to the policy do not signiﬁcantly
differ from the original policy. Another policy gradient
technique is trust region policy optimization (TRPO) [44],
which aims to maximize the policy function by limiting
policy updates to a trust region. This helps to prevent
excessive policy changes during each iteration.
3.3.3 Actor-critic methods
A hybrid approach that combines aspects of policy-based
and value-based techniques. Actor-critic architecture is
made up of two primary parts: actor and critic. Firstly, the
actor is the policy function, which chooses actions in a
speciﬁc state to govern the agent’s behavior and must be
learned by the actor. Regularly, a neural network is used to
implement it, which receives the state as input and returns
the probability distribution across the actions. Secondly,
the critic is the value function, which calculates the pro-
jected cumulative reward of adhering to a speciﬁc policy,
which must be learned by the critic. By assessing the
morality of the actor’s behavior, it gives the actor feedback.
Hence the actor concentrates on understanding a good
policy and the critic evaluates the player’s activities; the

3.3.4 Multi-agent RL
The majority of the above-mentioned methods are built on
MDP models, which depend on the availability of state
information about environments. However, in the real
world, some of the information in states can be private or
need cooperation and communication between different
agents; this type is called partially observable MDPs
(POMDPs) [1]. In such cases, the environmental states are
hidden, and DRL agents can only make decisions based on
their observations. Multi-agent DRL (MARL) is introduced
to tackle this problem. In MARL, several agents are
working together to perform long-term performance opti-
mization in POMDPs [49]. MARL scenarios can be
thought of as multiplayer competition and cooperation. For
example, in the case of the MEC environment, each end
device or edge node can act as an agent to make decisions
that optimize network performance. Thus, MARL can be
useful in the case of the MEC networks, as they have the
same distributed nature. Moreover, it offers a promising
solution for high-dimensional MDPs or POMDPs, partic-
ularly in IoT applications. The training process of MARL
can be done on centralized or distributed schemas. The
main algorithms in this ﬁeld are MARL [50] and
MADDPG [51]. A further discussion of MARL solutions is
provided in sub Sect. 6.2.

5.1 Content caching
This subsection analyzes RL-based mechanisms for content
caching to keep popular content closer to users. A further
discussion is provided about caching strategies, and the
reviewed papers will be categorized based on them. The
caching strategies are non-cooperative caching and coop-
erative caching.
5.1.1 Non-cooperative caching
In this scheme, each edge server ﬁnds its optimal caching
decision independently of the decisions of other nodes [58].
Edge server can predict which content will be accessed
most frequently in the future. It can increase cache hit rates
and overall system speed. It includes several steps: (1)
Predict content popularity, to forecast which content will
be popular in the future, machine learning models are
trained on historical access patterns. These models can
account for several variables, including the user’s location,
the time of day, and the qualities of the material. (2)
Content ranking, the server can give priority to caching the
most relevant content by using machine learning algo-
rithms that rate content according to projected popularity.
(3) Adaptability, ML caching can adjust to shifting trends
in user behavior and the popularity of content, guaranteeing
the cache’s continued efﬁcacy over time.
Wei et al. [59] handled the issues of joint content
caching, computation ofﬂoading, and radio resource allo-
cation, and proposed a joint optimization solution for the
fog-enabled IoT. They used an actor-critic reinforcement
learning framework to solve the optimization problem to
minimize the average end-to-end delay. Qian et al. [60]
consider cache optimization for both users and BSs one by
one. Then, the paper proposed a hierarchical reinforcement
learning (HRL) to coordinate these two optimization sub-
problems. The value function approximation Q-learning
and a DQN were used to solve these two subproblems
accordingly.
A software-deﬁned IC-IoT architecture was presented
by Yang et al. [61] to provide caching and computing
functionalities in IoT networks. The authors created a joint
resource scheduling technique based on this architecture.
Finally, a novel deep Q-learning technique was proposed to
address the resource scheduling issue. Then, they demon-
strated through the simulation that the suggested strategy
outperforms the current approaches in terms of reward and
static action value. In-EdgeAI [62] handled the main
optimization problems of MEC, namely computing, cach-
ing, and communication problems. The introduced frame-
work integrates both DRL and federated learning (FL)
techniques to optimize the system’s performance.
Elgendy et al. [63] formulated an efﬁcient model for
task ofﬂoading and caching integration. Q-learning and
DQN algorithms are proposed to reduce the total overhead
of time and energy. Meanwhile, an edge-enabled IoT sys-
tem is considered in [64], focusing on the joint caching and
computing service placement problem. To tackle this
problem, the paper presented a weight-averaged twin-Q-
delayed (WATQD) that uses the twin-delayed (TD) and
DDPG.
5.1.2 Cooperative caching
In contrast with the non-cooperative caching scheme, the
cooperative scheme, sometimes known as collaborative
caching, assumes that the edge servers cooperate and col-
laborate to store and serve cached content [26, 65]. They
communicate with each other to determine the best
placement of content and optimize caching strategies. In
order to determine which content to cache, edge servers
work together to consider global optimization factors such
as maximizing cache hit rates or lowering latency. More-
over, cooperative caching emphasizes the rule of content

Sun et al. [93] tried to minimize the average task latency
and task discard rate in time-varying multi-server MEC.
For this purpose, they proposed a computational ofﬂoading
method based on the DQN of multi-branch networks,
called BDQN. They converted the action generation net-
work into a multi-branch network structure to achieve a
linear increase in the number of network outputs. DRLCO
[94] tackled the MEC system with a server and multiple
mobile devices that need to perform computation tasks
with priorities. The algorithm jointly decided the ofﬂoading
decision, the CPU frequency, and the power transmitted for
computation ofﬂoading. The problem was formulated as a
long-term mixed-integer linear programming problem (LT-
MILP) to model a tradeoff between delay and energy.
DRLCO is decomposed of two parts. Initially, to handle the
power scheduling process, a DDPG based approach is used
to reduce the energy consumption of MDs by scheduling
the transmit power and CPU frequency of the MDS. Sec-
ondly, for task ofﬂoading, a double DQN was adopted to
reduce the execution delay of tasks by making ofﬂoading
decisions for computing tasks. Ullah et al. [95] presented a
double DQN algorithm that made ofﬂoading decisions by
considering resource utilization, task constraints, and the
current status of the edge-cloud network.
Sellami et al. [96] considered a massive IoT edge net-
work. The authors propose a DRL approach that combines
SDN and blockchain to ensure energy efﬁciency, reliabil-
ity, and low latency in a massive 5G IoT network. Task
scheduling, which is located in the SDN controller, is a
service that efﬁciently distributes tasks coming from
mobile IoT applications to be processed in the edge nodes.
It is the service that takes ofﬂoading decisions. The A3C
model was developed to solve the task scheduling problem
to maximize the capacity of task processing requests while
guaranteeing low latency and energy-saving. Moreover,
they extend their work in [97] and add blockchain systems
to provide secure and conﬁdent communication in the
SDN-enabled IoT network. ECO-SDIoT [98] is another
solution to consider SDEdge. ECO-SDIoT considered load
balancing between edge servers and made the ofﬂoading
decision of computing tasks to the most suitable edge
server according to the global states, task requirements, and
reward.
The tasks generated from users’ devices can have
deadline constraints that need to be executed before that
time. The computation ofﬂoading algorithm should apply
some priorities to handle such tasks as fast as possible. Ale
et al. [99] proposed an end-to-end DRL model to maximize
the number of computational tasks with deadline con-
straints and minimize energy consumption, respectively.
With the same perspective, work in [100] examined a
multiuser, multi-server MEC system with both real-time
and non-real-time tasks. POTD3 (partially observable twin
delayed DDPG) was presented to solve the problem. Fur-
thermore, the authors suggested using dynamic voltage and
frequency scheduling (DVFS), which allowed a mobile
device to modify the frequency of its CPU to maximize
energy efﬁciency.
The previous methods consider user devices with inde-
pendent task applications that can be executed locally on
the device, MEC server, or on the cloud. The following
solutions consider the other types of application tasks and
the dependent tasks that need to be handled. Table 4 shows
a summary of all centralized-based full computation
ofﬂoading. In order to minimize the costs associated with
transmission and processing, Wang et al. [101, 102]
introduced a new DRL-based ofﬂoading framework, which
can efﬁciently learn the ofﬂoading policy uniquely by
utilizing a sequence-to-sequence (S2S) neural network.
They assume that tasks are dependent and model it as
DAG. The DAG is then converted into task sequences
which have also been fed into the encoder and decoder of
S2S. Finally, it outputs the action for each task and feeds
the action as the input of the next step. Tang et al. [103]
suggested an RL-based multi-job dependent task ofﬂoading
approach. A job can be generated by mobile users, and it
contains one or more tasks with or without dependency. To
tackle the dependency problem, a graph convolutional
network (GCN) was created to extract the dependency
information between jobs. SACDTO [104] was designed

depending on the latest completion time and the latest
execution time.

5.3 Resource management
In this section, we will cover resource management from
the service provider’s perspective. Table 7 shows a sum-

MEC have two objectives: (1) enabling more users to
connect to edge servers to improve the QoS of users, and

limitation of edge server resources, efﬁcient resource

fulﬁll task requirements from user devices.
5.3.1 Edge server placement
User devices can ofﬂoad their application tasks to edge
servers. Thus, the application performance can be greatly
increased with the right edge server placement plan. The
issue of the edge server placement problem (ESPP) is
determined by selecting the ideal number and arrangement

issue. The servers’ locations are not stated in the MEC

servers in a way that satisﬁes computational needs while
keeping costs down. Moreover, an improper arrangement
of edge servers causes signiﬁcant workload imbalances
among servers and lengthy access delays [57]
Luo et al. [132] proposed a DQN solution for ESPP and
used it with a real dataset from Shanghai Telecom. The

deviation indicate better placement performance.
Another work focuses on the internet of vehicles (IoV)

leverages the DQN algorithm. The objective was formu-

5.4 Mobility management
To address (RQ8) question about mobility issues. We
discuss the mobility problem and mobility-aware solution
based on DRL algorithms in this section. MEC enables
users to ofﬂoad their application tasks to edge servers to
improve the quality of service (QoS) of mobile users and to
support a scalable internet of things (IoT) architecture by
handling time-sensitive applications such as healthcare,
smart cities, and so on. It is challenging to guarantee ser-
vice continuity because of the mobility of mobile users and
the constrained coverage of edge servers, which can lead to
severe network performance degradation or even the sus-
pension of ongoing edge services. Because the user may
move while the resource-intensive tasks are being off-
loaded [146]. Other problems include how to minimize
service outages during migration, and cooperatively allo-
cating compute and communication resources.
In this context, two problems need to be taken into
consideration: service migration and service placement.
Service migration is the stateful migration of user appli-
cations where the application can run on a virtual machine
(VM) or container on an edge server [147]. A mobile user
reserves internal state data on an edge server. After the
movement of the user, the current services can either
continue to run on the current edge server, and exchange
data with a mobile user through the core network or other
edge servers, or the services are migrated to another edge
server that covers the new area. While service placement is
the second problem, which is where to migrate and locate
service without violating load balancing on other edge
servers and to meet service requests [148]. In the former
two scenarios, it is obvious that the migration process is a
costly operation as it involves data transmission cost and
migration cost to transfer a huge volume of data (i.e., in
MBs or GBs). Therefore, the migration rate should be
minimized.
Recently, many mobility-aware solutions have been
proposed because mobility can affect several aspects: such
as computation ofﬂoading and resource allocation. Mobil-
ity-aware solutions can improve task migration time, and
study the interplay of MEC parameters such as capabilities
of the target MEC host, etc. [16]. Mobility models can be
used to mimic the movements of mobile users concerning
their location, velocity, and direction over some time.
Which includes software-deﬁned networking (SDN) mod-
els, stochastic models, random walk models, and user
movement tracking (UMT) based [146]. Table 8 summa-
rizes the literature in this section.

6.1 Proposed DRL algorithms
In this subsection, we review the DRL algorithms used by
authors in the surveyed papers above as shown in Fig. 6.
As shown in the ﬁgure, the ﬁrst three places go to value-
based methods. DQN is the most used algorithm in 31
papers. DDPG follows DQN in second place with 15
papers, then double DQN with 12 papers.
Value-based methods such as Q-learning, DQN, and
DDPG train a value function that calculates the expected
return or future reward of each state or state-action pair
rather than the use of an explicit policy. A deep neural
network that receives the state or state action as input and
outputs a scalar value is typically used to represent this
value function. Next, the agent behaves either epsilon-
greedily or greedily, depending on the value function and a
tradeoff between exploration and exploitation.
Value-based methods have many advantages, including
being able to learn deterministic policies that are optimal
for exploitation and deterministic environments; they are
reliable and easier to implement than popular policy-based
methods such as PPO or A2C. Moreover, they can leverage
prior knowledge or constraints by shaping the reward
function or the value function. They can also converge
faster to a global optimum [1].

6.2 Model approach
In this subsection, we will investigate model approaches
that are used in proposed papers (RQ4). Mainly, we have
two approaches: centralized and distributed approaches. As
shown in Fig. 7, centralized approaches are the most used,
and it has 58% over 42% for distributed approaches.
Centralized approaches depend on model training on
cloud or edge servers. Then the trained model is used to
optimize the problem and achieve the goal of the authors.
On the other hand, the distributed approach has two
ways of implementing: multi-agent RL (MARL) or feder-
ated learning (FL) with DRL [167].
In MARL frameworks, instead of having a single agent
interact with the environment, now we have multi-agents.
MARL considers the action policies of other agents during
training and the agents learn in cooperative strategies. They
adopted centralized training with a decentralized execution
method. MARL provides more ﬂexible and adaptive
recovery strategies, as agents can learn and adjust their
actions based on the current situation. It also shows great
potential in dealing with high-dimensional MDPs or
POMDPs, especially in many IoT applications [1].
FL is well suited for edge computing applications and
can leverage the computation power of edge servers and
the data collected on widely distributed edge devices
[168, 169]. FL can offer a promising solution for mitigating
the problems of unwanted bandwidth loss, data privacy,
and legalization [170]. FL enables decentralized architec-
ture, which is better than centralized architecture, as it is
suitable for MEC networks that involve several UEs and
ENs. Figure 8 shows FL architecture. It is a technique for
training neural networks across multiple devices. A single
global neural network is kept on a central server in this
processing approach. The neural network’s training set of
data is typically heterogeneous and is stored locally across
several nodes. The private dataset is maintained on each
node side. During a single synchronization, each node
calculates the updated weight based on the weight that is
present at time t and its private dataset.

7.6 Application partitioning
In edge computing, computation ofﬂoading has garnered a
lot of interest in resource scheduling. One portion of a task
can be computed locally, and the other part can be off-
loaded to ENs or other nodes for processing. In most of
previous publications, it is considered that the ofﬂoaded
portion of a task is indicated by an ofﬂoaded ratio. The
resource scheduling process is to determine an optimal
ofﬂoaded ratio and other optimization variables. Once the

as discussed before: full ofﬂoading and partial ofﬂoading.

dependent tasks is to effectively extract the key features of
task dependency. Resource scheduling algorithms’ goal is
to minimize the time to complete a task. However, due to
dependency on subtasks and the dependency between the
input of one subtask and the output of another. Now,
resource allocation should consider not just the number of
allocated resources but also the starting point of the allo-
cated time slot [54].

8 Conclusion
Multi-access edge computing is a promising solution for
many problems of user devices with limited resources.
MEC can offer resources, namely communication, com-
putation, and caching. It can support executing numerous
IoT applications and real-time applications that require
intensive processing or have delay constraints. Despite this,
as many devices are connected to networks and ofﬂoad
their intensive tasks to edge servers resource scheduling
problems rise and become more complex.
In this survey paper, we analyze and summarize the
recent literature on resource scheduling in the MEC sys-
tem. First, we overview DRL algorithms and the advan-
tages of DRL methods compared to traditional approaches.
Then, we investigate MEC architecture and classify the
problem into three research aspects, namely, content
caching, computation ofﬂoading, and resource manage-
ment. Moreover, we classify and compare 95 articles from
2019 to 2023. Articles proposed DRL solutions for
resource scheduling based on two approach modes: cen-
tralized and distributed. In our classiﬁcation, we highlight
the DRL technique that was used, how the problem was
formulated, what objectives are to be achieved, and the
tools and datasets that were used to build the model.
Finally, metrics were used by authors to evaluate their
work. The summarization of reviewed papers is presented
in Tables 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8.
Furthermore, we investigate the issue of user mobility
and its effect on the resource scheduling model. Finally, we
discussed general challenges for future research such as
security and privacy, mobility awareness, load balancing,
QoS concerns, scalability, and application partitioning.
Each challenge is addressed and discussed then several
ways are proposed to handle it.

Abstract: Multi-access edge computing (MEC) brings many services closer to user devices, alleviating the pressure on resource- constrained devices. It enables devices to ofﬂoad compute-intensive tasks to nearby MEC servers. Hence, improving users’ quality of experience (QoS) by reducing both application execution time and energy consumption. However, to meet the huge demands, efﬁcient resource scheduling algorithms are an essential and challenging problem. Resource scheduling involves efﬁciently allocating and managing MEC resources. In this paper, we survey the state-of-the-art research regarding this issue and focus on deep reinforcement learning (DRL) solutions. DRL algorithms reach optimal or near- optimal policies when adapted to a particular scenario. To the best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst survey that speciﬁcally focuses on the use of RL and DRL techniques for resource scheduling in multi-access computing. We analyze recent literature in three research aspects, namely, content caching, computation ofﬂoading, and resource management. Moreover, we compare and classify the reviewed papers in terms of application use cases, network architectures, objectives, utilized RL algorithms, evaluation metrics, and model approaches: centralized and distributed. Furthermore, we investigate the issue of user mobility and its effect on the model. Finally, we point out a few unresolved research challenges and suggest several open research topics for future studies.
